title: Inserting antibiotics into complex broken bones
official: Determining the feasibility of a randomised controlled trial of implanting local antibiotic carriers in the management of complex orthopaedic trauma (IMPACT)
summary:
Background and study aims
Broken bones, also called fractures, are very common and affect people of all ages. They usually happen after an accident, such as a fall or road traffic collision. Some fractures heal well without an operation, but others need surgery to put the broken bones back into position. Surgeons may use metal plates, screws or rods to hold the bones in place while they heal.
Most operations to fix fractures are successful, but there is always a risk of complications. One of the most serious complications is infection. If an infection develops, patients may experience more pain, slower healing, a longer stay in hospital and the need for additional operations. Infections are more common following complex fractures. These may occur after serious accidents and can cause damage to a joint, as well as to the muscles and skin surrounding the broken bone.

During surgery, patients are normally given antibiotics into a vein. These antibiotics circulate around the body in the blood and help prevent infection at the site of the operation. It may also be possible to reduce the risk of infection by placing additional antibiotics directly into the fracture during surgery. These antibiotics are contained within a paste that can be inserted into the bone by the surgeon.

A large study is needed to find out whether adding local antibiotics reduces the risk of infection after complex fractures. Before this larger study can take place, a smaller feasibility study is needed to determine whether enough patients can be recruited and followed up, whether the treatment can be delivered as planned and whether the information needed for the larger study can be collected.

The main aim of the IMPACT study is therefore to find out whether it is possible to carry out a larger randomised study comparing local antibiotics with standard hospital treatment.

Who can participate?
Patients aged 16 years or older may be able to participate if they have a complex fracture of the tibia, which is the larger bone in the lower leg, and require an operation. This includes:
-Open fractures of the tibia, where the skin has been broken
-Complex fractures involving the upper part of the tibia near the knee
-Complex fractures involving the lower part of the tibia near the ankle

Patients will not be able to participate if, for example, they have an allergy or another reason why they cannot receive gentamicin, which is the antibiotic contained within the local antibiotic treatment. 

What does the study involve?
The study will take place in at least three NHS hospitals in England. Patients who agree to participate will be allocated at random to one of two treatment groups. Random allocation means that a computer decides which treatment each patient receives. This helps make the groups as similar as possible, apart from the treatment being studied. Half of the patients will receive standard hospital treatment, including antibiotics given into a vein. The other half will receive standard hospital treatment and additional antibiotics placed directly into the fracture during surgery. The local antibiotic treatment is a paste called CERAMENT G, which contains the antibiotic gentamicin. Patients will not be told which group they have been allocated to during the study. The surgeons and clinical team will know because they need to provide the treatment safely.

After surgery, all patients will receive the usual care provided by their hospital. The study team will collect information about the operation, recovery, possible infections, wound problems, further operations and time spent in hospital.
Participants will also be asked to complete questionnaires about their health, mobility and recovery. Follow-up will mainly take place at approximately 30 and 90 days after surgery. The study team may also review the patient’s medical records for up to 12 months to identify any later complications.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants may not receive any direct benefit from taking part. The information collected may help researchers plan a larger study and may improve the treatment of patients with complex fractures in the future.
All participants will receive the usual antibiotics and surgical care provided by their hospital.
CERAMENT G is already used within the NHS for some patients. However, as with any treatment, there are possible risks. These may include an allergic reaction to gentamicin, wound leakage or other complications related to surgery. The clinical team will monitor participants closely and will treat any complications in the usual way.
Taking part will also require some additional time to complete study questionnaires and speak with members of the research team. Participation is voluntary. Patients can decide not to take part or can withdraw from the study without affecting the standard of care they receive.

Where is the study run from?
The study is being coordinated by the University of Oxford and Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (UK).

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2026 to July 2028.

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research through a Doctoral Research Fellowship. The University of Oxford is the study sponsor and is responsible for overseeing the study.

Who is the main contact?
Mr Jamie Hind, jamie.hind@ndorms.ox.ac.uk
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1.	Aged 16 years or over
2.	Sustained a complex tibia fracture, which includes; open tibia fractures , closed Proximal segment tibia fractures (e.g. Tibial Plateau fractures) and closed Distal segment tibia fractures (e.g. Pilon/Plafond fractures)
3.	In the opinion of the treating clinician, would benefit from surgical management
4.	Attended the treating hospital within 72 hours of the injury
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Known allergy to gentamicin, or other contraindication 
2.	Pre-existing infection/osteomyelitis at the fracture site
